L47: Sep 22, 2026
L48: # National leaders and lawmakers celebrate Governor Newsom’s signature on the most comprehensive data center laws in the nation
L49: 
L50: SACRAMENTO – Yesterday, Governor Gavin Newsom signed cite26†the most comprehensive data center laws in the nation , providing communities more control on water, electricity, and land use. These new laws will help protect California’s innovation economy while giving Californians a stronger voice on proposed projects in their communities.
L51: Here’s what leaders are saying about the historic legislation:
L52: Senator Jerry McNerney (D-Pleasanton): “Communities across California and the nation are increasingly concerned about skyrocketing utility bills due to the rapid growth of data centers and their energy use. Data centers not only use large amounts of electricity, but they can cause utilities to make infrastructure upgrades to handle the increased power demand.
L53: Governor Newsom’s signing of my SB 1168 helps ensure that data centers absorb the costs of their energy use and any utility upgrades they require, not ratepayers.”
L54: Senator Steve Padilla (D-San Diego): “These are some of the nation’s strongest data center ratepayer protections – stopping Big Tech from sticking California families with the bill for their data centers while ensuring all local voices have a say on these projects and they comply with our air, water, and climate standards. Big Tech keeps promising to be good neighbors and these laws now make those promises legally enforceable.
L55: No more saying one thing in the White House and doing the opposite in our local communities. I’m incredibly grateful to Governor Newsom for signing these nation-leading protections for ratepayers and our environment into law.”
L56: Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan (D-Orinda): “Thank you, Governor Newsom, for signing AB 1577. AB 1577 is a huge step forward in prioritizing California’s ratepayers and helping California move toward a more sustainable energy future.
L57: This will give us the transparency needed for the state and local communities to be in control of the future here in California. It allows us to understand the growing energy demands of data centers, the impact on local communities, plan for that growth, and protect California’s ratepayers. California continues to put our people first.”
L58: Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur (D-Hollywood): “As California continues to lead the world in innovation, we must ensure that working families and small businesses are not left footing the bill for data centers’ enormous energy demands.
L59: Assembly Bill 2383 ensures these large energy users pay their fair share of the costs needed to serve them, protects ratepayers from unfair cost shifts, and helps California responsibly plan for the future of our electrical grid while reducing electricity costs for consumers.”
L60: Assemblymember Diane Papan (D-San Mateo): “These bills are essential for the future of water management in California and I am grateful for the Governor’s partnership. In signing both of these bills, Governor Newsom has positioned California to balance innovation and sustainability.”
L61: Mark Toney, Executive Director, TURN: “Collectively these measures protect ratepayers from subsidizing the significant energy consumption of data centers, ensuring that the data centers pay upfront for the extra infrastructure that must be built to operate them, and pay their fair share for wildfire mitigation and other ratepayer-funded programs. We are grateful for the Governor’s leadership to hold these data centers accountable.”
L62: Sam Uden, Co-founder and Managing Director, Net-Zero California: “Managing data center-driven load growth is one of the most consequential energy issues facing the nation today. California policymakers have met the moment with a robust set of protections that first and foremost prevent data centers from shifting costs onto ratepayers. These bills also lay a foundation to turn data center growth into an opportunity — bringing new energy supply onto the grid and strengthening reliability.
L63: This package represents a sophisticated response to a critical public issue: we don’t need moratoriums if we have the leadership to put strong protections in place while capturing the broader economic and technological benefits of data centers.”
L64: Linda Serizawa, Director, California Public Advocates Office: “By enacting this package, the Governor and Legislature have put much-needed transparency requirements and ratepayer protections in place for data centers in California. Californians deserve greater visibility into the energy and water demands of these projects, and existing customers should not have to shoulder unreasonable costs to accommodate that demand.
L65: Better reporting, planning, and protections to keep those costs from being passed on to ratepayers will provide greater accountability for this growing industry.”
L66: Victoria Rome, Director of California Government Affairs at Natural Resources Defense Council Nonprofit: “Some of the wealthiest companies in the world are building data centers, and they can afford to cover their own costs instead of passing them on to California families. These laws help protect ratepayers from higher bills driven by increased demand from data centers, steer data centers towards new clean energy, and give communities more information before a project moves forward.
L67: Governor Newsom and our state leaders have set a model for the nation: data centers must pay their own way and respect the people who live next door.”
L68: Andy Wunder, Senior Western Advocate, E2 (Economy+Environment): “California has long demonstrated that climate leadership and economic growth go hand in hand.
L69: These responsible data center development laws build on that principle – protecting our grid and advancing energy affordability while keeping California at the forefront of technological innovation.  With clear and enforceable guardrails, businesses and residents won’t front the cost of data center growth and development will not be at the expense of California’s ambitious climate and clean energy goals.”

L47: Sep 21, 2026
L48: # Governor Newsom signs most comprehensive data center laws in the nation, providing communities more control on water, electricity, and land use
L49: 
L50: What you need to know: Governor Newsom today signed seven bills to strengthen California’s approach to data centers — requiring data centers to report about water and electricity use. The bills help protect California’s innovation economy while ensuring Californians have a say regarding proposed projects in their communities.
L51: SACRAMENTO – As Donald Trump dismisses Americans’ concerns about the growing emergence of data centers in their communities, California is enacting new laws to increase transparency and prevent working families from shouldering the costs. The laws give communities more information about energy, water, workforce, and land use for proposed data centers so they can better weigh the economic costs and benefits of such projects.
L52: While the Trump administration moves toward deregulation, communities are left to deal with the consequences — higher electricity demand, grid constraints, water use, and pollution. Today we are once again laying the groundwork for a stronger approach, because we know that we don’t have to sell out Californians or sacrifice our well-being to innovate and succeed. California has proven that time and time again.
L53: With these laws, we are ensuring that Californians remain in the driver’s seat — and that those profiting from data centers aren’t doing so at our expense.
L54: 
L55: Governor Gavin Newsom
L56: As the innovation economy continues to grow, data centers are being presented as a solution, but with little thought or oversight of what that means for nearby communities. Today’s announcement helps communities take a stronger role in the decision-making process and protects working families from shouldering the cost as industry reaps massive profits.
L57: California is implementing stronger reporting requirements, giving communities more information about the water, electricity, and land use of proposed data centers. With these new laws, California is helping to ensure that communities have more information they need to decide whether data centers are right for them, including:
L58: ⚡Electricity, by making data centers pay their fair share of grid update costs, while preventing cost shifts to low-income customers. The new laws will also ensure data centers comply with California energy procurement requirements, bring new clean energy supply onto the grid, and pay for any upgrade costs. This legislation will prevent data centers from shifting costs onto everyday ratepayers.
L59: ​​🚰Water, by requiring that proposed data centers provide information to local governments and water suppliers about water use, supply, efficiency and drought planning. Any upgrades needed to supply water would be paid for by the data center.
L60: 🏞️Land use, by making data centers ineligible for blanket environmental exemptions and instead requiring data centers to demonstrate that the project will not shift costs to ratepayers, but will meet state standards on energy, water, and fuel consumption before any judicial streamlining could be approved.
L61: 
L62: The Governor has signed the following bills:
L63: 
L64:   * AB 1577 by Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan (D-Orinda). Data centers: reporting
L65:   * AB 2383 by Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur (D-Hollywood). Electricity: data centers.
L66: 
L67:   * AB 2469 by Assemblymember Diane Papan (D-San Mateo). Data centers: water use disclosures.
L68: 
L69:   * AB 2619 by Assemblymember Diane Papan (D-San Mateo). Water resources: data center.
L70: 
L71:   * SB 886 by Senator Steve Padilla (D-San Diego) and Senator Jerry McNerney (D-Pleasanton). California Technology Innovation and Ratepayer Protection Act.
L72:   * SB 887 by Senator Steve Padilla (D-San Diego). California Environmental Quality Act: environmental leadership development projects: data centers: geothermal power plant projects.
L73: 
L74:   * SB 1168 by Senator Jerry McNerney (D-Pleasanton). Data centers: Rate structures.

Chaptered (9/21/2026)

Existing law vests the Public Utilities Commission with regulatory authority over public utilities. Existing law authorizes the commission to fix the rates and charges for every public utility and requires that those rates and charges be just and reasonable.

This bill would require the commission to assess opportunities for rate structures to ensure data centers pay a reasonable share of their costs associated with transmission and distribution needs, ensure that data centers pay for their proportionate share of load increases and procurements needed to reliably serve their loads while maintaining consistency with the applicable integrated resource planning requirements, and alleviate cost pressures on residential ratepayers.

L41: CHAPTER 440
L42: An act to add Article 10.5 (commencing with Section 901) to Chapter 4 of Part 1 of Division 1 of the Public Utilities Code, relating to energy.
L43: 
L44: [ Approved by Governor  September 21, 2026. Filed with Secretary of State  September 21, 2026. ]
L45: ## LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
L46: 
L47: SB 1168, McNerney. Data centers: rate structures.
L48: 
L49: Existing law vests the Public Utilities Commission with regulatory authority over public utilities. Existing law authorizes the commission to fix the rates and charges for every public utility and requires that those rates and charges be just and reasonable.
L50: This bill would require the commission to assess opportunities for rate structures to ensure data centers pay a reasonable share of their costs associated with transmission and distribution needs, ensure that data centers pay for their proportionate share of load increases and procurements needed to reliably serve their loads while maintaining consistency with the applicable integrated resource planning requirements, and alleviate cost pressures on residential ratepayers.
L51: Vote: MAJORITY   Appropriation: NO   Fiscal Committee: YES   Local Program: NO
L52: 
L53: * * *
L54: ## The people of the State of California do enact as follows:
L55: ### SECTION 1.
L56: 
L57:  The Legislature finds and declares all of the following:
L58: 
L59: (a) Data centers’ energy use is rapidly increasing across the nation. In California, the Independent System Operator expects energy use to grow by 2.3 gigawatts by 2030. The Pacific Gas and Electric Company alone had about 2,300 megawatts of applications for data center capacity in 2024.
L60: (b) Demands for energy by data centers are growing at the same time as energy prices for Californians are also growing at an unprecedented rate due to factors such as wildfire risk, extreme heat, and the state’s transition to clean energy.
L61: (c) In order to facilitate data center growth in California while simultaneously retaining reasonable electricity and natural gas rates for all Californians, it is critical to ensure that data centers are contributing back to rate stabilization for all by helping pay down the largest driver of utility rates.
L62: ### SEC. 2.
L63: 
L64:  Article 10.5 (commencing with Section 901) is added to Chapter 4 of Part 1 of Division 1 of the Public Utilities Code, to read:
L65: 
L66: ##### Article  10.5. Data Centers
L67: ###### 901.
L68: 
L69:  As part of a new or existing proceeding, the commission shall assess opportunities for rate structures to do all of the following:
L70: 
L71: (a) Ensure data centers pay their reasonable share of costs associated with transmission and distribution needs, regardless of whether the data centers interconnect at the transmission or distribution level.
L72: (b) Ensure data centers pay for their proportionate share of load increases and procurements needed to reliably serve their loads while maintaining consistency with the applicable integrated resource planning requirements.
L73: 
L74: (c) Alleviate cost pressures on residential ratepayers, including, but not limited to, customers enrolled in the California Alternate Rates for Energy program described in Section 739.1 and the Family Electric Rate Assistance program described in Section 739.12.

L39: Assembly Bill No. 1577
L40: 
L41: CHAPTER 434
L42: An act to add Sections 7927.303 and 65909.3 to the Government Code, and to add Section 25302.10 to the Public Resources Code, relating to energy.
L43: 
L44: [ Approved by Governor  September 21, 2026. Filed with Secretary of State  September 21, 2026. ]
L45: ## LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
L46: 
L47: AB 1577, Bauer-Kahan. Data centers: reporting.
L48: 
L49: Existing law establishes the State Energy Resources Conservation and Development Commission and vests the commission with various responsibilities with respect to developing and implementing the state’s energy policies. Existing law requires the commission to biennially adopt an integrated energy policy report, as specified, and to make the reports accessible to state, local, and federal entities and to the general public.
L50: This bill would require the commission to establish a process for the owner or operator of a data center, as defined, to submit specified information to the commission, including, among other information, the data center’s location and size, the data center’s power usage effectiveness, as defined, and the quantity of fuel consumed by onsite generators or other fuel-based energy systems, as specified.
L51: The bill would require the owner or operator of a data center to submit the required information in the manner and timeframe specified by the commission. The bill would require the commission, beginning with the 2029 integrated energy policy report, and in subsequent biennial reports thereafter as determined by the commission, to include an assessment of electrical load trends for data centers, as provided.
L52: The bill would require the commission to annually publish the information submitted in an anonymized and aggregated format on its internet website. The bill would require the commission to establish a process for the owner or operator of a data center to identify information that the owner or operator claims is exempted or prohibited from disclosure pursuant to federal or state law, as provided.
L53: The bill would require the owner or operator of a data center, upon applying for a discretionary permit, entitlement, or land use authorization required for the construction or operation of the data center, to submit to the applicable local agency, as defined, specified information, including the expected annual energy consumption, as specified, and the expected sound levels attributable to the operation of the data center, as provided.
L54: The bill would authorize the local agency to use this information for various purposes, including, but not limited to, land use planning, infrastructure planning, energy supply assessment, and environmental review.
L55: The bill would exempt a publicly funded research facility, public safety facility, publicly funded national security facility, publicly owned facility, or other utility facility, as provided, from the above-described provisions.
L56: 
L57: The bill would prohibit the commission or a local agency from disclosing the information described above in a manner that would result in the disclosure of personally identifiable information or energy consumption data for a data center customer, as provided.
L58: Existing constitutional provisions require that a statute that limits the right of access to the meetings of public bodies or the writings of public officials and agencies be adopted with findings demonstrating the interest protected by the limitation and the need for protecting that interest.
L59: 
L60: This bill would make legislative findings to that effect.
L61: 
L62: Vote: MAJORITY   Appropriation: NO   Fiscal Committee: YES   Local Program: NO
L63: 
L64: * * *
L65: ## The people of the State of California do enact as follows:
L66: 
L67: ### SECTION 1.
L68: 
L69:  Section 7927.303 is added to the Government Code, to read:
L70: ###### 7927.303.
L71: 
L72:  (a) The State Energy Resources Conservation and Development Commission or a local agency shall not disclose information submitted pursuant to Section 65909.3 of this code or to subdivision (b) of Section 25302.10 of the Public Resources Code in a manner that would result in the disclosure of personally identifiable information or energy consumption data for a specific data center customer.
L73: (b) Subdivision (a) does not supersede, preempt, or otherwise limit any reporting, disclosure, or public access requirements imposed by any other law or regulation, including requirements to report the same information to the same public entities.
L74: (c) Any designation or labeling of information submitted pursuant to Section 65909.3 of this code or to subdivision (b) of Section 25302.10 of the Public Resources Code as confidential, proprietary, or otherwise restricted for purposes of this section shall not require the same designation or labeling of that information pursuant to any other law or regulation.
L75: (d) The disclosure or sharing of information pursuant to Section 65909.3 of this code or to subdivision (b) of Section 25302.10 of the Public Resources Code does not constitute a waiver of any attorney-client privilege, work product protection, or trade secret protection that might otherwise exist with respect to the information.
L76: 
L77: (e) For purposes of this section, “data center” has the same meaning as defined in Section 25302.10 of the Public Resources Code.
L78: ### SEC. 2.
L79: 
L80:  Section 65909.3 is added to the Government Code, to read:
L81: ###### 65909.3.
L82: 
L83:  (a) Upon applying for a discretionary permit, entitlement, or land use authorization required for the construction or operation of a data center, the owner or operator of the data center shall submit to the applicable local agency an estimate of all of the following information, to the extent applicable to the proposed facility:
L84: 
L85: (1) The expected annual energy consumption of the data center, expressed in kilowatthours.
L86: (2) The expected annual quantity of electricity generated onsite, including both behind-the-meter primary and backup power generation, separated by generation type and expressed in kilowatthours.
L87: 
L88: (3) The expected average and maximum sound levels attributable to the operation of the data center, expressed in A-weighted decibels, measured at the point along the property boundary where the average sound level attributable to the operation of the data center is highest.
L89: (b) The information submitted pursuant to subdivision (a) shall be based on the best available estimates at the time of submission.
L90: 
L91: (c) A local agency may use the information submitted pursuant to this section for various purposes, including, but not limited to, land use planning, infrastructure planning, energy supply assessment, and environmental review.
L92: (d) This section does not apply to a publicly funded research facility, public safety facility, publicly funded national security facility, publicly owned facility, or other utility facility, including, but not limited to, a facility operated for the purpose of providing telecommunications services to the public by a terrestrial facilities-based telecommunications, cable, or internet service provider.
L93: 
L94: (e) For purposes of this section, all of the following definitions apply:
L95: (1) “Applicable local agency” means a city, county, or city and county, that has discretionary land use or permitting authority over the construction or operation of a data center.
L96: 
L97: (2) “Data center” has the same meaning as defined in Section 25302.10 of the Public Resources Code.
L98: 
L99: (3) “Owner or operator” has the same meaning as defined in Section 25302.10 of the Public Resources Code.
L100: ### SEC. 3.
L101: 
L102:  Section 25302.10 is added to the Public Resources Code, to read:
L103: ###### 25302.10.
L104: 
L105:  (a) For purposes of this section, all of the following definitions apply:
L106: 
L107: (1) (A) “Cooling degree day” means the number of degrees by which the average outdoor air temperature for a given day exceeds 65 degrees Fahrenheit.
L108: 
L109: (B) If the average outdoor air temperature for a given day does not exceed 65 degrees Fahrenheit, the number of cooling degree days for that day shall be zero.
L110: (2) (A) “Data center” means, except as provided in subparagraph (B), a facility, or part of a facility, that houses computing infrastructure, including graphics and central processing units, servers, storage devices, networking equipment, and associated power and cooling systems, for the primary purpose of processing, storing, or distributing electronic data.
L111: 
L112: (B) “Data center” does not include a facility with an electrical capacity of less than 10 megawatts.
L113: (3) “Owner or operator” means the individual or entity responsible for overseeing daily operations for the entire data center facility, regardless of the individual parties that may rent or host equipment at the facility.
L114: 
L115: (4) “Power usage effectiveness” means a ratio of the total energy consumption of a data center to the energy specifically used by the information technology equipment housed in that data center.
L116: (b) (1) The commission shall establish a process for the owner or operator of a data center to submit all of the following information to the commission upon energization of the data center and following any substantive change to information previously submitted pursuant to this paragraph:
L117: 
L118: (A) The name of the data center.
L119: 
L120: (B) Any physical addresses associated with the operation of the data center.
L121: 
L122: (C) The name of, and contact information for, the owner or operator of the data center.
L123: (D) The year and month that the data center began operating.
L124: 
L125: (E) The total floor area of the data center, expressed in square feet.
L126: 
L127: (F) The floor area of the data center occupied by information technology equipment, expressed in square feet.
L128:
